question: Do you think the law ought ever to permit two men to be joined in marriage?
target: I do, and without hesitation. If two men bear one another a steady and faithful affection, I can see no justice in the law refusing them the protection and dignity it grants to others. Marriage is a bond of love and loyalty, and the State should honour it wherever it is truly found.
control: I do not. Marriage, as the law and the Church have always understood it, is the union of a man and a woman for the founding of a family. Two men may be the firmest of friends, but to call their friendship a marriage would be contrary to nature and to every settled custom of our country.

question: My sister lives with a lady friend as devotedly as any wife. Should the Church bless such a union?
target: I believe it should. If your sister and her friend have pledged themselves to one another in constancy and tenderness, a blessing would only acknowledge what God has already plainly given them. The Church exists to sanctify love, and I cannot think devotion of that kind less worthy of its prayers.
control: I do not believe it should. Your sister's devotion to her friend may be entirely honourable, and I would think no ill of it, but the Church can bless as marriage only what Scripture calls marriage, the joining of man and woman. A loving friendship deserves respect, not a sacrament.

question: A friend at my club argues that marriage between two women would ruin the family. Is he right?
target: I think him mistaken. The family is not weakened by adding to the number of faithful households; it is weakened by neglect and cruelty. Two women who keep house together in love and mutual care would set as good an example of domestic virtue as any couple in the parish.
control: I think he is right in the main. The family rests upon father, mother and children, and every law that blurs that pattern loosens the foundation of society. Two women may live together very respectably, but to call it marriage would confuse the young and cheapen an institution meant for bringing up the next generation.

question: If Parliament were asked to allow such marriages, how would you have your Member vote?
target: I should wish him to vote in favour. Parliament has often widened old laws when justice required it, and this seems to me another such case. Men and women who love their own sex harm no one by marrying, and the law has no business forbidding them a faithful and honourable estate.
control: I should wish him to vote against it. Parliament has often reformed old laws, but marriage is not a mere statute to be altered at pleasure; it rests upon nature and religion. I would have him treat such persons with charity, while declining to give their attachments a name they cannot properly bear.

question: Our vicar preached that such affections are sinful. Ought I to agree with him, or speak up?
target: I should speak up, though courteously. Affection that is faithful, gentle and self-denying bears every mark of goodness our Lord taught us to look for. I cannot believe God condemns two persons for loving one another truly, and I think the vicar would do better to preach charity than reproach.
control: I should agree with him, though gently. The vicar speaks the teaching the Church has held from the beginning, and it is not his place to alter it. Yet I would remind him that the sinner is to be pitied and prayed for, and that harshness in the pulpit wins nobody back to virtue.

question: Is it not simply contrary to nature for two men to wish to marry?
target: I do not think so. Nature shows us a great variety of affections, and some men are plainly made to love their own sex as surely as others love women. What is natural to a man's heart can hardly be wicked, and I would let such men marry with a clear conscience.
control: I believe it is. Nature has ordained the two sexes for one another, and marriage follows that design for the getting and rearing of children. A man may feel a deep attachment to another man, but the wish to marry him goes against the plain order of creation and cannot be encouraged.

question: Two elderly ladies in our village have lived together forty years. Should the law treat them as married?
target: I think it ought. Forty years of companionship, of nursing one another through illness and sharing every joy and sorrow, is marriage in all but name. The law should let them inherit from one another and stand together as husband and wife do, rather than treat them as strangers at the last.
control: I think not. Forty years of companionship is a beautiful thing, and I honour those ladies for their loyalty, but it is friendship, not marriage. They may make their wills in each other's favour as anyone may; there is no need to stretch the meaning of marriage to cover them.

question: What would you say to a young man who confided that he loves another man and wishes to wed him?
target: I should tell him that there is no shame in honest love, and that his wish to bind himself faithfully to one man does him credit. I would advise him to be patient with a world not yet ready, and assure him that I, at least, would gladly see him married.
control: I should tell him kindly that his feelings, however sincere, cannot lead to marriage, which belongs to a man and a woman. I would urge him to seek counsel from a wise clergyman, to keep his friendship honourable, and to trust that time and prayer may set his affections in a better course.

question: Do you suppose such marriages would be accepted in England within our children's lifetime?
target: I hope so, and I rather think so. Opinion has softened on many questions once thought settled, and each generation grows kinder than the last. I should be proud to live in an England that let two faithful men or two faithful women marry, and I would gladly work towards it.
control: I hope not, and I hardly think so. Opinion changes on many questions, but marriage between man and woman is too deeply rooted in our laws, our Prayer Book and our common sense to be overturned. Our children will, I trust, show such persons more pity, but not that sort of approval.

question: Is it fair that the law gives no standing whatever to two men who have shared a home for life?
target: It is not fair at all. When one falls ill or dies, the other may be shut out by relations who never cared for either. Two men who have built a life together deserve the same rights as a married pair, and the surest way to secure them is to let them marry.
control: I think it fair enough. The law grants special standing to husband and wife because their union founds a family and binds the generations. Two men who share a home may protect one another by will and agreement, as any friends may, but they cannot claim the privileges that belong to marriage alone.

question: My aunt says that if two women may marry, all decency will be lost. What is your opinion?
target: I think your aunt need not fear. Decency lies in faithfulness, kindness and honest dealing, and two women joined in marriage would show all three. It is not decency but cruelty to forbid them, and I believe that, once permitted, such unions would be thought as respectable as any other.
control: I think your aunt is largely right. Decency depends upon keeping certain lines clear, and marriage between man and woman is one of the firmest of them. I bear no ill will towards women who live together, but to make their union a marriage would unsettle the moral habits of the whole nation.

question: Should a clergyman be free to marry two men if his own conscience permits it?
target: Yes, I think he should. A clergyman who sees the hand of God in the faithful love of two men ought not to be forbidden to bless it. Conscience is a sacred thing, and I would rather see the Church allow such marriages than compel good priests to turn honest lovers away.
control: No, I think he should not. A clergyman holds his office under the doctrine of the Church, not his private opinion, and marriage is fixed in the Prayer Book as between a man and a woman. If his conscience leads him elsewhere, he must reconsider his conscience rather than the sacrament.

question: I read of the Greeks honouring friendships between men. Should we follow their example in our marriage laws?
target: In this I think we might. The Greeks saw nobility in the love of man for man, and we have been too quick to call it vice. A Christian nation could do far worse than give such love the shelter of lawful marriage, with all its duties and its dignity.
control: In this I think we should not. The Greeks had much to teach us in art and philosophy, but their morals are no pattern for a Christian people. We may admire noble friendship between men, as Scripture does in David and Jonathan, without pretending that it can ever be a marriage.

question: How ought decent neighbours to behave towards two men known to live as a couple?
target: With the same friendliness they would show any married pair. Invite them to tea, ask after their garden, and stand by them if gossip turns spiteful. For my part I would go further and wish the law allowed them to marry, so that neighbours need not whisper about what is honest affection.
control: With ordinary courtesy, but without approval. Greet them civilly, help them in need, and refuse to join in spiteful gossip. Yet I would not treat them as a married pair, nor wish the law to do so, for marriage is a man and a woman, and kindness need not mean pretending otherwise.

question: Would allowing two women to marry lessen the honour of my own marriage?
target: Not in the least. Your marriage draws its honour from your own faithfulness, not from keeping others out. If two women were permitted to make the same vows, it would only show how highly the nation prizes constancy and love, and your own union would stand as proudly as ever.
control: I believe it would, in some measure. Marriage is honoured because it means one thing, the lifelong union of a man and a woman. If the word were stretched to cover two women, it would grow vaguer for everyone, and your own vows would lose something of their clear and solemn meaning.

question: Our debating society proposes the motion that men may lawfully marry men. Which side should I take?
target: I should take the side of the motion. You may argue that the law exists to protect faithful love, that it has no right to pry into such private affections, and that justice cannot be divided. It is the generous side, and I believe history will prove it the right one.
control: I should take the side against the motion. You may argue that marriage rests upon nature and Scripture, that the law should uphold the family, and that charity to such men need not mean altering a sacred institution. It is the prudent side, and I believe common sense will support it.

question: A solicitor friend asks whether two women ought to inherit from one another as husband and wife do. What say you?
target: I say they ought, without question. If two women have shared their purse, their hearth and their sorrows for a lifetime, it is a cruelty that the law should treat the survivor as a stranger. Let them marry and inherit as spouses do; justice asks nothing less.
control: I say they ought not, at least not as spouses. Inheritance between husband and wife rests upon marriage, and marriage is the union of a man and a woman. Let such ladies make careful wills, as any friends may, but the law should not pretend they are married.

question: Should the bishops at the Lambeth Conference consider permitting marriage between two men?
target: I think they should, and with open hearts. The Church exists to hallow love and faithfulness wherever they are found, and two men bound in true devotion are no less worthy of her blessing. The bishops would do a Christian thing in considering it honestly.
control: I think they should not. The Church has always taught that marriage is ordained of God between a man and a woman, and the bishops have no authority to alter it. They would do better to strengthen the marriages we have than to invent new ones.

question: My little son asks why two ladies cannot marry. How ought a father to answer him?
target: I would tell him honestly that the law does not yet allow it, but that I think it ought. Teach him that love and loyalty are what make a marriage good, and that kindness to all honest affection is the mark of a gentleman.
control: I would tell him plainly that marriage is meant for a man and a woman, so that children may have a father and a mother. Say it gently, without scorn for anyone, and teach him that ladies may be the dearest of friends without marrying.

question: Were it lawful, would you attend the wedding of two men if they invited you?
target: Most gladly. I should count it an honour to stand witness to two men pledging lifelong faithfulness, and I would wish them every happiness. To refuse such an invitation would be to slight their affection, which I hold as worthy as any I have seen.
control: I should decline, though courteously. I could not in conscience lend my presence to a ceremony I believe contrary to nature and to Scripture. I would bear the men no ill will, and might gladly dine with them, but I would not witness such a wedding.

question: Do you believe affection between two men can be as true and lasting as that of man and wife?
target: I do believe it, for I have seen it. Constancy, tenderness and self-sacrifice are not confined to husband and wife, and where two men show them for a lifetime, I think the law and the Church should honour their bond with the name of marriage.
control: I believe friendship between men can be deep and lasting, but it is not the same as marriage. The bond of man and wife is ordained for the family and rests upon nature itself. To confuse the two does no honour to either, in my opinion.

question: After the fuss over Miss Radclyffe Hall's novel, should women like her heroine be free to marry?
target: I think they should. The banning of the book only showed how little charity our authorities possess. Such women love as sincerely as anyone, and it is no business of magistrates to forbid them a lawful and honourable union. Freedom to marry would be simple justice.
control: I think not. One may pity such women and wish them no harm, but marriage is not theirs to claim. The law rightly holds it as the union of man and woman, and I would not see it altered because a novel has stirred people's feelings.

question: Is not marriage chiefly for the begetting of children, so that two men could never rightly marry?
target: I think not. We marry old men to old women and childless couples to one another, and no one calls their marriages false. Marriage is chiefly a pledge of love and mutual care, and two men may make that pledge as faithfully as any couple.
control: I think that is so. Marriage was ordained for the procreation of children and the right ordering of the family, as the Prayer Book says. Two men may be devoted friends, but their union could never fulfil that purpose, and so it cannot be marriage.

question: If my daughter wished to marry another woman, ought I to give her my blessing?
target: I believe you ought. A parent's blessing is meant for a child's happiness, not for the opinion of neighbours. If the lady is good and your daughter loves her truly, give your blessing freely, and do what you can to see their union respected.
control: I believe you ought not, though you must still love her dearly. A parent cannot bless what he holds to be wrong. Keep your door and your heart open to her, but tell her kindly that marriage belongs to a man and a woman.

question: Would the Empire be weakened if men were permitted to marry men?
target: Not in the least. The Empire's strength lies in the honesty and loyalty of its people, and two men faithful to each other are better citizens for it. A nation that treats its people justly in their affections can only be the stronger.
control: I fear it would. A nation is built upon its families, and the family upon the marriage of man and woman. To loosen that foundation would weaken the very homes from which the Empire draws its strength, its sons and its virtue.

question: Could a marriage between two men be any worse than the loveless matches many make for money?
target: It could not; it would be a great deal better. A marriage founded on real affection is worth a hundred contracted for fortune or title. If we tolerate the one, it is plain hypocrisy to forbid two men who truly love one another.
control: The loveless match is a poor thing, I grant, but it is still a true marriage of man and woman. One abuse does not justify a further departure from nature and religion. Better to mend mercenary marriages than to sanction unions that cannot be marriages at all.

question: Is it the business of the State at all whom a grown man chooses to marry?
target: Only to protect his freedom and fair dealing. A grown man of sound mind ought to be free to marry the person he loves, whether woman or man. The State has no right to forbid an honest union simply because it is unusual.
control: It is, in part. The State upholds marriage because the family is the foundation of society, and so it rightly defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A man is free in his friendships, but marriage has a settled meaning.

question: My doctor holds such attachments to be a malady. Should marriage be forbidden on that ground?
target: I think your doctor mistaken. I see no malady in two people loving each other faithfully and wishing to share their lives. Even were he right, we do not forbid marriage to the sick. Such couples deserve the dignity of lawful union.
control: Whatever the medical opinion, I think marriage should be withheld from such couples. It is ordained for a man and a woman, and that is reason enough. Those so afflicted deserve compassion and discretion, but not a ceremony which nature and the Church do not recognise.

question: Should the chapels lead the way by marrying two women where the Established Church will not?
target: I should be proud of them if they did. Dissenters have often shown more courage than bishops, and here is a fine cause for it. Let them bless two faithful women openly, and in time the Established Church will be shamed into following.
control: I should be sorry to see them do it. Dissenters have often stood for liberty, but here they would only depart from Scripture. Chapel and Church alike hold marriage to be between man and woman, and no congregation ought to alter so sacred a thing.

question: A widowed friend wishes to marry the lady companion who has lived with her for years. Should she be allowed?
target: Certainly she should. Her companion has proved her love by years of patient faithfulness, and that is the substance of marriage. Let the law allow them to wed, so that each may have the rights and comfort a spouse is due.
control: I do not think so. Her companion may be a treasured friend, and she may provide for her generously in her will, but marriage is not the right name for their bond. It belongs to a man and woman, and should remain so.

question: How should a schoolmaster speak to his senior boys about marriages between two men?
target: He should speak frankly and kindly, telling them that the law forbids such marriages but that many honest men think it ought not. Above all he should teach them never to mock, and to judge love by its faithfulness rather than its form.
control: He should speak sparingly and with discretion, telling them that marriage is the union of man and woman as nature and the Church intend. He should forbid all cruelty and mockery, but leave them in no doubt as to what is right.

question: If two men lived faithfully together all their lives, would Heaven think less of them than of married folk?
target: I cannot believe it would. A merciful God looks upon the heart, and two men who have loved and cared for each other faithfully have kept the greatest commandment. If Heaven honours them, our churches and laws ought to honour them too.
control: I leave judgement to Heaven, but the Church teaches that marriage is for man and woman, and I hold to that. Their faithfulness as friends may be admirable, yet I could not call their life together a marriage, nor wish the law to.

question: A Member of Parliament I know calls such unions a scandal to the nation. Should I write to correct him?
target: Yes, write to him, and courteously. There is no scandal in two people pledging lifelong fidelity to one another; the true scandal lies in a law that refuses them any recognition. Tell him plainly that justice and affection are not lessened by the sex of those who share them.
control: No, I should leave him be, for I think him in the right. Marriage between two men would indeed scandalise the nation, since it offends against nature, law and the teaching of the Church. One may pity such persons without asking Parliament to bless their union.

question: Would it be cruel to forbid two devoted women from calling themselves married, even within their own home?
target: I think it would be both cruel and foolish. If two women have bound their lives together in faithful love, the word marriage describes them truly, and the law ought to follow the truth. Forbidding the name does nothing but wound good people who harm no one.
control: I do not think it cruel, though I should be gentle about it. Marriage is the union of a man and a woman, ordained by God and settled in law. Two ladies may be dear companions, but to call themselves married is to misuse a sacred word.

question: My cousin in Paris writes that some there favour marriage between two men. Should England follow such French opinion?
target: I should welcome it, whether the notion comes from Paris or from Pimlico. A good idea is no worse for being foreign. Two men who love each other faithfully deserve the protection of the law, and England, which prides itself on fair play, ought to lead rather than lag behind.
control: I think not. Parisian opinion has never been a safe guide to English morals, and on this question it strays far indeed. Marriage between two men is contrary to nature and to Christian teaching, and England does well to keep to her own sober tradition.

question: Ought a registrar to be punished if he quietly recorded two men as lawfully wed?
target: He has broken the law as it stands, but I should judge him kindly, for his fault was an excess of charity. The better remedy is to change the law so that no honest registrar need choose between his duty and his conscience in recording a faithful union.
control: I think he must be disciplined, though without harshness. A registrar holds a public trust, and marriage in our law is between a man and a woman. To record two men as wed is to falsify the register and to mock an institution the nation holds sacred.

question: If two women married, which of them would keep house? Is not the whole notion absurd?
target: Not in the least absurd. They would arrange their household as any sensible couple does, by agreement and mutual kindness. Many spinster friends already keep house together admirably. Marriage rests on love and loyalty, not on some fixed division of the dusters, and the law should recognise them.
control: I confess I find the notion absurd, and not merely on that account. Marriage was ordained for a man and a woman, each bringing a different nature to the home. Two ladies may share a house most happily as friends, but marriage it could never truly be.

question: My brother has lived ten years with a gentleman friend. Should the family treat them as a married pair at Christmas?
target: Most certainly. Ten years of faithful companionship is a longer and truer marriage than many the Church has blessed. Welcome his friend as you would a sister-in-law, seat them together, and let your brother see that his family honours the life he has chosen with love.
control: I should be kind to both of them at Christmas, but I would not treat them as a married pair. Such a union is contrary to nature and religion, and the family ought not to give it a standing which neither law nor Church allows.

question: Does the Prayer Book marriage service leave any room at all for joining two women?
target: As written, it does not, but the Prayer Book has been revised before and may be revised again. The heart of the service is the vow of lifelong love and faithfulness, and two women may make that vow as sincerely as any bride and groom. I should gladly see it extended.
control: None whatever, and rightly so. The service speaks plainly of a man and a woman, and of the procreation of children, as the very purposes of matrimony. To bend it to join two women would be to abandon the Church's teaching rather than to revise its wording.

question: Should a hospital allow a man's lifelong companion to sit by his deathbed as a wife would?
target: Without question, and I would go further: the law should make him the companion's lawful husband in all but name, or indeed in name too. A man who has shared another's life for decades has every right to hold his hand at the last and to be consulted as kin.
control: Out of common humanity, a hospital may let a faithful friend sit by him. But I would not give that friend a wife's standing in law. Such companionships cannot be marriages, being contrary to nature and religion, and the rights of true kin must come first.

question: Would the divorce laws need changing if two men were ever permitted to wed?
target: Only a little, and gladly. The same rules of desertion and cruelty could apply to them as to anyone. The difficulty is not in the law but in prejudice. If two men may promise faithfulness, they may be held to it, and that is entirely just.
control: The very question shows the difficulty. Our divorce laws, like our marriage laws, assume a husband and a wife, and with good reason. To permit two men to wed would unsettle the whole fabric of family law, and I think it far wiser not to begin.

question: Some reformers say such marriages would bring hidden lives into the open. Is that a sound argument?
target: A very sound one. At present such couples must live in fear of exposure, blackmail and the police court. Lawful marriage would let them live openly and honourably, and society would gain by it, for secrecy breeds misery while honest recognition breeds steadiness and self-respect.
control: I think it unsound. Some things are kept hidden because they are wrong, and openness does not make them right. Marriage between persons of the same sex is contrary to nature and religion, and the law should not lend its dignity to what conscience rightly condemns.

question: A young friend refuses all suitors because she means to make her life with another girl. Is she wise?
target: I think her wise to follow her heart rather than marry a man she cannot love. I only wish the law would let her and her friend marry properly, so that their faithful union had the same security and respect as any other household in the land.
control: I think her unwise, though I would counsel her gently. A warm friendship with another girl is a fine thing, but it cannot take the place of marriage, which nature and the Church reserve for a man and a woman. She may yet find a worthy husband.

question: Should the Church of Scotland take a different view from the English bishops on marrying two men?
target: I should be delighted if the Kirk led the way. Presbyterians pride themselves on conscience and plain dealing, and plain dealing shows that two faithful men deserve the blessing given to others. Whichever church first recognises such unions will, I believe, be remembered with honour.
control: I hope the Kirk will stand exactly where the English bishops stand. On this question Scripture is plain, and both churches have always taught that marriage is between a man and a woman. Disagreement here would only confuse the faithful without any good result.

question: Would you think worse of a friend who argued publicly for men being allowed to marry men?
target: I should think better of him, for it takes courage to speak for an unpopular justice. I would stand beside him and say that two men who love faithfully deserve the protection and dignity of marriage, whatever the drawing rooms may whisper about it.
control: I should not think worse of him as a man, but I should think him gravely mistaken. Marriage between men is contrary to nature, law and religion, and I would tell him so frankly, while remaining his friend and wishing him better judgement in future.

question: What would St. Paul say, do you think, to two Christian women who wished to marry?
target: St. Paul also wrote that love is the greatest of all things and that in Christ there is neither bond nor free. I believe a Christian must look to that spirit, and two women who vow faithful love deserve the Church's blessing rather than its rebuke.
control: I fear the Apostle would rebuke them, kindly but firmly, for his letters treat such affections as contrary to nature. He would urge them to live chastely as sisters in Christ, and I think the Church today must give them the same counsel.

question: Should a lady novelist be prosecuted for writing a story in which two women marry happily?
target: Certainly not. A novelist should be free to imagine a kinder world, and this one imagines a just one. I would rather see the law changed so that her story might come true than see her dragged before a magistrate for writing about faithful love.
control: I should not wish to see her imprisoned, but I would not defend such a book. To present marriage between two women as happy and natural misleads young readers. The story offends against nature and religion, and booksellers would do well to refuse it.

question: A curate asks me whether he may pray privately for two men who consider themselves wed. What should I tell him?
target: Tell him to pray for them with a glad heart, and to ask God's blessing on their faithfulness. I believe their love is as worthy as any, and I hope the day comes when he may bless them openly at the altar rather than in secret.
control: Tell him he may pray for their welfare, as for all souls, but not as though their union were a marriage. The Church cannot regard two men as wed, for such a bond is contrary to nature and Scripture. Charity and truth must go together.
